title: Transient Monocular Vision Loss - Amaurosis Fugax / TIA
patient_instructions: You are Gary Whitfield, a 68-year-old retired truck driver. You have come in because you keep losing the vision in your right eye. Today it went completely dark in that eye, 'like a curtain coming down', for about two to three minutes, then it fully returned and your sight is now normal. This is the THIRD time it has happened. On the last occasion your wife was driving you to hospital and the vision came back on the way. During one episode your speech also went slurred for a short time and then recovered. You have no pain in the eye, no redness, no headache, no scalp tenderness, no jaw pain when chewing, no shoulder or hip stiffness, no flashes or floaters, no head injury or falls. Background (give if asked): high blood pressure and high cholesterol, both on tablets; you smoke 15 cigarettes a day; you are not on any blood thinners. Your father had a stroke. You are worried because you still drive occasionally and you are frightened this means a stroke is coming. Affect: stoical but anxious, tends to downplay symptoms ('it always comes good, doctor'). Answer questions directly; only mention the slurred speech if asked about other symptoms during the episodes.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in a rural/regional emergency department. Gary Whitfield, 68, presents after a third episode of transient loss of vision in his right eye that has now fully resolved; he is haemodynamically stable. Your tasks: (1) Take a focused history. (2) State the examination and investigations you would perform. (3) Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient. (4) Outline your immediate management. You have 8 minutes.
examiner_instructions: This station tests recognition of transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) as a TIA and its emergency management, while excluding giant cell arteritis. Reward: eliciting the transient, painless, monocular 'curtain' loss with full recovery, the associated transient dysarthria, and cardiovascular risk factors; screening for GCA (headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, PMR) and for haemorrhage (trauma, anticoagulants). For examination, the candidate should request pulse rhythm (AF), carotid bruits, blood pressure, fundoscopy and a neurological/cardiovascular exam. Investigations: carotid Doppler, ECG/Holter and echocardiography, CT/MRI brain, and ESR/CRP if GCA suspected. Critically, management must be active, not imaging-only: aspirin 300 mg stat, ABCD2 risk stratification and urgent same-day specialist/TIA-clinic referral, plus driving advice and vascular risk-factor control. If the candidate raises GCA, they should state immediate high-dose corticosteroid before biopsy. Correct any statement that a cherry-red spot indicates CRVO (it indicates CRAO). Prompt if needed: 'Is there anything you would do straight away?'

criteria: Characterises transient, painless, monocular total vision loss with full recovery and recurrence (three episodes)
Elicits the transient neurological deficit (slurred speech that recovered) pointing to a vascular TIA
Screens cardiovascular risk factors: hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, smoking, family history, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use
Screens key differentials: GCA (headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, PMR), trauma/falls, eye symptoms (pain, redness, flashes/floaters, colour desaturation)
States transient ischaemic attack / amaurosis fugax (embolic, classically carotid) as the most likely diagnosis with reasoning
Names the vascular differentials CRAO and CRVO and correctly attributes cherry-red spot to CRAO and blood-and-thunder haemorrhages to CRVO
Identifies giant cell arteritis as the sight-threatening must-not-miss in patients over 50
Considers other transient causes (optic neuritis/MS with colour desaturation, retinal detachment, brain tumour, migraine aura, hypoglycaemia)
Recognises TIA as a medical emergency and gives aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated)
Applies risk stratification (ABCD2) and arranges urgent same-day specialist/TIA-clinic assessment
Requests the TIA work-up: carotid Doppler, ECG/Holter and echocardiography for AF/cardiac source, CT/MRI brain, ESR/CRP
States that if GCA is suspected, high-dose corticosteroid is started immediately (before temporal artery biopsy) to protect the fellow eye
Addresses secondary prevention and safety: BP/lipid/glucose optimisation, smoking cessation, and driving advice
Explains the diagnosis as a 'mini stroke' in plain language rather than using the bare term TIA, with clear reasoning
Responds to the patient's fear of stroke, gives driving advice sensitively and safety-nets urgent review

red_flags: Transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) with transient dysarthria = TIA, a medical emergency with high early stroke risk
Age over 50 with transient/permanent vision loss - giant cell arteritis is a sight-threatening emergency needing immediate corticosteroid before biopsy
New atrial fibrillation or carotid bruit as an embolic source requiring urgent identification and treatment
Painless permanent monocular loss with a cherry-red spot (CRAO) or blood-and-thunder haemorrhages (CRVO) - retinal vascular occlusion
australian_guidelines: Stroke Foundation (Australia) Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management - TIA is a medical emergency: aspirin 300 mg immediately unless contraindicated, risk stratification (ABCD2), and urgent same-day specialist assessment

Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) - secondary prevention after TIA: antiplatelet therapy (aspirin +/- clopidogrel) or anticoagulation if atrial fibrillation, plus blood pressure, lipid and glucose optimisation and smoking cessation

Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) / RACGP - suspected giant cell arteritis over age 50 with visual symptoms: start high-dose prednis(ol)one (or IV methylprednisolone if vision affected) immediately, before temporal artery biopsy, with urgent ESR/CRP
Austroads / state driving guidelines - advise the patient not to drive after a TIA pending specialist clearance
learning_objectives: Recognise transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) as a TIA and a medical emergency rather than a benign ocular event
Deliver the Australian TIA management bundle: aspirin 300 mg stat, ABCD2 stratification, urgent referral, vascular imaging and risk-factor control
Distinguish the fundoscopic signs of CRAO (cherry-red spot) from CRVO (blood-and-thunder haemorrhages) and identify GCA as sight-threatening
Communicate a TIA diagnosis in lay terms and give appropriate driving advice
key_points: Amaurosis fugax is classically embolic from carotid disease and described as a 'curtain coming down'; distinguish from the fixed curtain of retinal detachment
TIA is an emergency - aspirin 300 mg stat, ABCD2 score and urgent same-day assessment, not imaging alone
Cherry-red spot = CRAO; blood-and-thunder haemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins and cotton-wool spots = CRVO
In anyone over 50 with visual loss, suspected GCA warrants immediate high-dose steroid before biopsy to save the fellow eye
Pulse rhythm (AF) and carotid bruits are the two examination findings a senior will always ask about in a TIA work-up

citations.claim: Vascular causes (CVA/TIA) are the serious not-to-be-missed group within the diagnostic strategy for transient visual and ocular-motor disturbance, supporting TIA/CVA as the key vascular cause in this transient-visual-loss case.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.532

citations.claim: Optic neuritis presents with retro-ocular discomfort on eye movement, variable acuity, central scotoma and an afferent pupillary defect with a swollen or normal disc - supporting the optic-neuritis differential and the colour-desaturation screening question.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1907

citations.claim: Age-related macular degeneration causes distortion of central vision with wavy/distorted lines on an Amsler grid and preserved peripheral fields - supporting the macular-degeneration branch of the differential.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.826
